His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. And when was she going to be told? If nothing had happened, she would have to have a serious talk with Minta. The Owl and the Poker—yes, they would be displeased if they heard (and they were sure to hear) that Minta, while staying with the Ramsays, had been seen et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. “He wore a wig in the House of Commons and she ably assisted him at the head of the stairs,” she said over to herself, hauling them up out of her memory with a phrase she had invented, on the way home from some party, to amuse her husband. Dear me, Mrs. Ramsay said to herself, how had those two ever produced such an unlikely daughter? This tomboy Minta, with a hole in her stocking? How did she survive in that ponderous atmosphere, where the maid was forever sweeping into a dustpan the sand the parrot had scattered, and conversation had shrunk almost entirely to that bird’s exploits—interesting, perhaps, but limited, when all was said and done? Naturally she had invited Minta to lunch, then tea, then dinner, and in the end to come and stay with them up at Finlay. That had caused some friction with the Owl, her mother, and led to more calls, and more conversation, and more sand, until, by the end of it, she had told enough lies about parrots to last a lifetime (as she had put it to her husband that night, on the way home from the party). Still, Minta came. … Yes, she had come, Mrs. Ramsay thought, feeling some thorn caught in the tangle of this thought; and when she worked it loose, she found that it was this. A woman had once accused her of “robbing her of her daughter’s affections”; and something Mrs. Doyle had said brought that accusation back to her. That she wanted to dominate, wanted to interfere, made people do what she wanted—that was the charge against her, and she thought it deeply unfair. Could she help how she looked? Nobody could say she went to any trouble to impress. She was often ashamed of how shabby she was. Nor was she domineering, nor tyrannical. It was truer where hospitals and drains and the dairy were concerned. About things like that she did feel passionately, and, given the chance, she would have liked to grab people by the scruff of the neck and make them see. Not one hospital on the whole island. It was a disgrace. Milk left on your doorstep in London that was actually brown with dirt. There ought to be a law against it. A model dairy and a hospital here—those were the two things she would have liked to do, with her own hands. But how? With all these children? Later, when they were older, maybe she would have time; once they were all at school.

before: Oh, but she never wanted James to get one day older, nor Cam either. These two she would have liked to keep just as they were, forever—demons of wickedness, angels of delight—and never watch them turn into long-legged monsters. Nothing could make up for that loss. Just now, when she had read James the line “and there were numbers of soldiers with kettledrums and trumpets,” and his eyes had darkened, she had thought: why should they grow up and lose all that? Of all her children he was the most gifted, the most sensitive. But every one of them, she thought, was full of promise. Prue was an absolute angel with the others, and these days, especially in the evenings, her beauty could take your breath away. Andrew—even her husband granted that he had an extraordinary gift for mathematics. And Nancy and Roger had both turned into wild creatures, running all over the countryside from morning till night. As for Rose, her mouth was too big, but she was wonderful with her hands. When they put on charades, it was Rose who made the costumes; she made everything; what she liked best was arranging things—tables, flowers, anything at all. Mrs. Ramsay didn’t like Jasper shooting birds; but that was only a phase; they all went through phases. Why, she asked, resting her chin on the top of James’s head, must they grow up so quickly? Why must they go off to school? She would have liked always to have a baby. She was never happier than with one in her arms. Then people could call her tyrannical, domineering, overbearing, whatever they pleased; she didn’t care. And as she touched his hair with her lips she thought, he will never be this happy again—but she stopped herself, remembering how angry her husband got when she said that. Still, it was true. They were happier now than they would ever be again. A tenpenny tea set could keep Cam happy for days. The moment they woke, she heard them stamping and crowing on the floor over her head. They came clattering along the passage. Then the door burst open and in they came, fresh as roses, wide-eyed, wide awake, as if coming into the dining room after breakfast—which they did every single day of their lives—were a real occasion for them. And so it went, one thing after another, all day long, until she went up to say good night and found them caught in their cots like birds netted among the cherries and raspberries, still inventing stories about some scrap of rubbish—something they had overheard, something they had found in the garden. They each had their little treasures. … And so she went downstairs and said to her husband, Why must they grow up and lose it all? They’ll never be so happy again. And he was angry. Why take such a gloomy view of life? he said. It isn’t sensible. For it was strange—and she believed it to be true—that for all his gloom and despair he was happier than she was, more hopeful on the whole. Perhaps it was that he was less exposed to human troubles. He always had his work to fall back on. Not that she was “pessimistic” herself, as he accused her of being. It was only that she thought life—and a small strip of time appeared before her eyes, her fifty years. There it lay in front of her—life. Life, she thought, but she didn’t finish the thought. She took a look at life, because she had a distinct sense of it there, something real, something private, which she shared with neither her children nor her husband. A kind of transaction went on between the two of them, with her on one side and life on the other. She was always trying to get the upper hand of it, as it was of her; and sometimes they held talks (when she sat by herself); there had been, she remembered, great scenes of reconciliation. But mostly, oddly enough, she had to admit that she felt this thing she called life to be terrible, hostile, ready to spring on you the moment you gave it the chance. There were the eternal problems: suffering; death; the poor. Even here there was always some woman dying of cancer. And yet she had told all these children, You shall go through with it. To eight people she had said it, relentlessly (and the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds). And for that reason, knowing what lay in store for them—love and ambition and being miserable and alone in dreary places—she often felt: Why must they grow up and lose it all? And then, brandishing her sword at life, she told herself, Nonsense. They’ll be perfectly happy. And here she was, she thought, sensing again how sinister life was, making Minta marry Paul Rayley. Because whatever she might feel about her own transaction—and she had been through things that needn’t happen to everyone (she didn’t name them, even to herself)—she was driven on, too fast, she knew, almost as if it were an escape for her as well, to declare that people must marry; people must have children.

before: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that begged off the scorn and anger of the world — she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? And on top of all this chaos Mr. Ramsay had stood up, pressed her hand, and said, “You will find us much changed,” and not one of them had stirred or spoken; they had sat there as if they had no choice but to let him say it. Only James (certainly the Sullen one) glowered at the lamp, and Cam wound her handkerchief round and round her finger. Then he reminded them that tomorrow they were going to the Lighthouse. They were to be ready in the hall at half past seven sharp. Then, with his hand on the door, he paused and swung round on them. Didn’t they want to go? he demanded. If they had dared to say no (he had some reason for wanting it), he would have hurled himself tragically backward into the bitter waters of despair. He had such a talent for gesture. He looked like a king in exile. James said yes, doggedly. Cam faltered more miserably. Yes, oh yes, they would both be ready, they said. On and on she wrote. At last she looked up at something floating in the sea. “Oh,” she said, “is it a lobster pot? Is it a boat turned upside down?” She was too nearsighted to see it, and at that Charles Tansley became as nice as he possibly could. He started playing ducks and drakes, skipping stones. What they talked about, she could not remember—only herself and Charles throwing stones, suddenly getting along very well, and Mrs. Ramsay watching. She had been very aware of that. before: But the dead, Lily thought—she had hit some snag in her design that made her stop and consider, stepping back a foot or so—oh, the dead! she murmured. You pitied them, you pushed them aside, you even felt a little contempt for them. They are at our mercy. Mrs. Ramsay has faded away and gone, she thought. We can overrule her wishes and improve away her narrow, old-fashioned ideas. She draws further and further away from us. Lily seemed to see her, mocking, at the far end of the corridor of years, saying the most unsuitable thing imaginable: “Marry, marry!” (sitting bolt upright early in the morning, as the birds began to chirp in the garden outside). And you would have to tell her, It has all gone against your wishes. They’re happy that way; I’m happy this way. Life has changed completely. At that, all of her, even her beauty, turned for a moment dusty and out of date. For a moment Lily, standing there with the sun hot on her back and the Rayleys summed up, triumphed over Mrs. Ramsay. Mrs. Ramsay would never know how Paul went to coffeehouses and kept a mistress; how he sat on the ground while Minta handed him his tools; how Lily stood here painting, and had never married—not even William Bankes.

before: She had an odd idea that he did hear, after all, the things she couldn’t say. He was an unreadable old man, with his yellow-stained beard and his poetry and his puzzles, sailing calmly through a world that met all his needs; it seemed to her that he had only to lower his hand where he lay on the lawn to fish up whatever he wanted. She looked at her picture. That, presumably, would have been his answer: how “you” and “I” and “she” pass and vanish; nothing lasts; everything changes; but not words, not paint. And yet it would be hung in the attics, she thought; it would be rolled up and tossed under a sofa. Even so, even of a picture like that, it was true. You could say of this scrawl—perhaps not of the actual picture, but of what it tried to do—that it “remained forever.” That was what she was going to say; or rather, since the words sounded too boastful even to her once spoken, she would hint it without words. But when she looked at the picture, she was surprised to find she couldn’t see it. A hot liquid filled her eyes (at first she didn’t think of tears); it left her lips firm, but it thickened the air and ran down her cheeks. In every other way she was in complete control of herself—oh yes! Was she crying for Mrs. Ramsay, then, without being aware of any unhappiness? She turned to old Mr. Carmichael again. What was it, then? What did it mean? Could things push their hands up and grab you? Could the blade cut, the fist clench? Was there no safety? No learning the world’s ways by heart? No guide, no refuge—was it all miracle, and leaping off the top of a tower into the air? Could it be that, even for older people, this was life?—startling, unexpected, unknown? For one moment she felt that if the two of them stood up, here and now on the lawn, and demanded an explanation—why was it so short, why so impossible to explain—and demanded it violently, the way two fully equipped human beings might speak who should have nothing hidden from them, then beauty would roll itself up; the space would fill; those empty flourishes would take shape; if they only shouted loudly enough, Mrs. Ramsay would come back. “Mrs. Ramsay!” she said out loud. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Tears were streaming down her face.
